doc.title: Dianne Reeves interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, October 13, 2001

title: Preparation, learning from Carmen McRae and Betty Carter
summary: Without jazz schools, she learned through experience, her uncle's insistence on preparation, and watching singers such as McRae and Carter.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: That’s interesting you say that you had your keys together and your whole thing. Do vocalists ever — I’m not sure how to even ask this question—
Do they ever feel pressured by instrumentalists to really, you know you better know your stuff here?

Well I think my uncle just always wanted me to be prepared. I guess they do, but my uncle always wanted me to be ready and be prepared, be able to communicate clearly my ideas and specifically what it was that I wanted to hear or what I wanted. And so that was the training early on. And you know I would go and I would listen to other vocalists too. Because at the time there was not a lot of, there weren’t a lot of schools for jazz, to study jazz music. So the way that you got it was through experience and through other musicians that would help you. At least that’s how I got it. And I would go and hear other singers. Like for instance I would go and hear Carmen McRae and she was very, very open, so I could ask her a lot of different questions about how she was approaching songs, who did this arrangement, why did she do it this way or — and you know she would tell me. And I remember the first time I saw Betty Carter it was the first time I’d ever seen a vocalist really stand inside of a band and allow the musicians to be these co- creators and really, really use their own personalities as part of the sound in a band. And I wanted to know how do you communicate those things? How do you do that? And I had my own bands early on, and I think that the biggest thing that helped me was the experience and just continuously learning to be very, very clear and to be able to articulate.

There’s a certain amount of physicalization that you do. When I think back of when I saw Betty Carter, I can almost see a nice comparison there. Just, I don’t know, the way you use your arms. It works.
